title: The Helping Relationship and the Values That Drive It
overview: This chapter describes how helpers should behave toward clients. It first examines the helping relationship: the relationship valued in itself (Rogers) versus as a means to an end, and the working alliance that unites both through collaboration on goals and tasks. It covers getting off to a good start, keeping the client's preferences central, the relationship as a forum for relearning, and relationship flexibility. It then sets out five values that drive helping: respect (the foundation value), empathy (the primary orientation value), proactive appreciation of diversity (culture, personal culture and multicultural competence), self-responsibility (the empowerment value, set within helping as social influence) and a bias for action (the outcome value, including behavioral activation and discretionary change). It ends with the shadow side: flaws of helpers and clients and the reality of incompetent helpers.
objectives: Compare the Rogerian, psychodynamic and means-to-end views of the helping relationship.
Define the working alliance and explain the principles that make it work in practice.
Describe how helpers can get off to a good start and keep clients' preferences central.
Explain how the relationship serves as a forum for relearning and why flexibility is essential.
Distinguish espoused values from values-in-use and explain why values are tools of the trade.
Explain respect and empathy as helping values and the behaviours through which they are shown.
Discuss culture, personal culture and the competencies needed for diversity-sensitive helping.
Explain helping as a social-influence process and the norms for client empowerment and self-responsibility.
Explain the bias for action, behavioral activation and discretionary change.
Identify shadow-side realities including helper and client flaws and incompetent helpers.

sections.heading: The Helping Relationship
sections.detailed:
Egan opens the chapter by saying that it is about how helpers should behave toward clients. He advises reading it quickly but thoughtfully first and then returning to it while working through Parts II and III of the book, because its suggestions are detailed and the student can easily get lost in them.

Everyone involved in helping, whether theoretician, researcher, practitioner or client, agrees that the client-helper relationship matters. The disagreement is about how the relationship should be described and how it should operate in practice. Some writers stress the relationship in itself; others stress the work that gets done through it. Some speak of a "relationship", others prefer "working alliance". Even where writers share a theme such as collaboration, they picture collaboration differently. Egan links this to the idea of uncertainty from Chapter 1: helping is not an exact science.

Egan therefore does not try to settle the debates. His aim is to give helpers a clinical feel for what a good relationship looks like and the behaviours that build a helping partnership. There is no single correct way to form a helping relationship. Although some basic principles exist, each helper and each client have to co-discover and co-develop the right way for their particular encounter.

He notes that a large body of research on the relationship has appeared over the past decade (Norcross), some of it contradictory, and that the APA Task Force findings were introduced in Chapter 1. Rather than review all of it critically, the chapter asks practical questions: what helpers and clients need to know about the relationship, how counsellors can bring clients into a collaborative relationship, and how to make sure the relationship serves life-enhancing outcomes.

Egan's own view is that research often just confirms common sense. Common sense is not a scientific term, but clients understand it, and related words such as prudence, judgement, practicality, wisdom and street smarts convey the idea. He admits that one person's common sense may not be another's, and jokes that common sense may not be all that common.
sections.simple: Everyone agrees the helper-client relationship matters, but people describe it differently: some focus on the relationship itself, others on the work done through it. Egan does not try to settle the debate. He wants helpers to get a practical feel for a good relationship, knowing that each helper and client must work out the right way together.
keyPoints: The chapter is about how helpers should behave toward clients.
Views differ: relationship in itself vs work done through the relationship; 'relationship' vs 'working alliance'.
Collaboration is a common theme, but writers define it differently.
There is no one right way; helper and client co-discover and co-develop the relationship.
Egan holds that much relationship research confirms common sense.

sections.heading: The Importance of the Relationship Itself
sections.detailed:
Any relationship, helping relationships included, can be understood by looking at what each party brings to the table and how these contributions interact. Helper and client each come with personality traits and a personal culture (explained later in the chapter) that shape how they form and keep relationships. Egan imagines the two meeting at a party or conference before therapy: neither would be acting from a role, and the relationship would depend on what each brought along. The point is that the human package each person carries into the session affects the helping relationship. Norcross reminds us that the relationship is wider and more inclusive than the working alliance alone. So the better both client and helper understand how they themselves build and maintain relationships, the better they might be at forming a working alliance; Egan stresses that the word is "might".

Most therapy approaches affirm the relationship's importance, but in different ways. Carl Rogers, a major pioneer of counselling and a representative of the humanistic-experiential approach, emphasised the quality of the relationship. He claimed that three helper conditions, unconditional positive regard, accurate empathy and genuineness, when offered by the helper and perceived by the client, were necessary and often sufficient for therapeutic progress. Through such a strongly empathic relationship, counsellors help clients understand themselves, release unused resources and manage their lives better. Rogers's work launched the client-centred approach.

Psychoanalytic and psychodynamic approaches see the relationship differently. For them transference and countertransference are central. These are complex, initially unconscious interpersonal dynamics between helper and client rooted in the past of the client and sometimes of the helper. Some argue that working through these murky dynamics is essential to successful outcomes.

The contrast is important for exams: Rogers treated the empathic relationship as a facilitative condition that makes change possible, not as a problem to be explored and resolved, whereas psychodynamic writers treat the relational dynamics themselves as material to be worked through.
sections.simple: Both helper and client bring their own personalities and personal cultures to the relationship, and this shapes it. Rogers said that unconditional positive regard, accurate empathy and genuineness are necessary and often sufficient for change. Psychodynamic approaches instead focus on transference and countertransference as issues to be resolved.
keyPoints: Each party 'brings to the table' personality traits and personal culture.
Norcross: the relationship is broader than the working alliance.
Rogers: unconditional positive regard, accurate empathy and genuineness are necessary and often sufficient.
Psychodynamic view: transference and countertransference are central and must be resolved.
Rogers saw the relationship as a facilitative condition, not a problem to explore.

sections.heading: The Relationship as a Means to an End
sections.detailed:
A second view holds that the relationship is very important but is still a means to an end. This fits the book's emphasis, from Chapter 1, that life-enhancing client outcomes are what helping is about. Tursi and Cochran observed that the cognitive-behavioural tasks of helping are carried out within a person-centred relational framework. On this view a good relationship is valuable because it is practical: it allows client and counsellor to do whatever work the chosen helping process calls for.

Practitioners who use cognitive and behavioural approaches, including the manualised treatments discussed in Part III, tend to hold this means-to-end view, although they are sensitive to relationship issues. They argue that overstressing the relationship is a mistake, because it hides the ultimate goal of helping, which is managing problem situations and developing life-enhancing opportunities.

Their position has two sides. A poor relationship will block the goal: the work will not succeed if the relationship is bad. But too much attention to the relationship itself can distract both client and helper from the real work that needs to be done. The relationship is therefore necessary but not the end product.

This view sits between the Rogerian emphasis on the relationship as healing in itself and a purely technical view of therapy, and it prepares the ground for the working-alliance idea that follows.
sections.simple: Here the relationship is important but mainly as a tool for getting the real work done. Cognitive-behavioural helpers say a bad relationship blocks progress, but focusing too much on the relationship distracts from solving the client's problems.
keyPoints: Relationship valued because it enables the work of helping.
Tursi and Cochran: cognitive-behavioural tasks done within a person-centred relational framework.
Typical of cognitive and behavioural approaches and manualised treatments.
Overstressing the relationship obscures the goal of problem management and opportunity development.
A poor relationship still prevents success.

sections.heading: The Relationship as a Working Alliance
sections.detailed:
Norcross defines the alliance as the quality and strength of the collaborative relationship between client and therapist. The term has a long history and many interpretations (Horvath and colleagues), but Egan uses it to combine the best of the two earlier views: the empathic relationship valued in itself and the relationship as a means to desired outcomes. Bordin defined the working alliance as client-helper collaboration based on agreement on the goals and tasks of counselling. Horvath and associates add a dynamic element: the alliance is an emerging quality of partnership and mutual collaboration that may form quickly or be nurtured over a longer time.

The collaborative nature of helping. In the alliance helpers and clients are collaborators. Helping is not something done to clients but a process both work through together (Frankel). Helpers do not cure patients. Both have work to do in the problem-management and opportunity-development stages, and both share responsibility for outcomes. Outcomes depend on the competence and motivation of each, and on the quality of their interaction. It is a two-person team effort; if either refuses to play or plays incompetently, the whole enterprise can fail.

Types of client collaboration. Bachelor, Laverdiere, Gamache and Bordeleau found three types. Active clients see themselves as playing a significant role in whether the work moves forward. Mutual clients acknowledge their own role but expect the therapist to play an equally active role. Therapist-dependent clients see collaboration as the therapist's beneficial interventions; about a third of clients were of this type, and Egan suggests it might better be called cooperation than collaboration.

Guiding principles for alliance behaviour. Because the alliance is an abstraction, it becomes real only through behaviour. Egan offers these principles, illustrated with Laura and her client Karl, a veteran:
- Alliances emerge. Do not try to build an alliance directly; make sure everything you do contributes to a spirit of collaboration, and the alliance grows.
- Track the client's evolving needs and wants. Understand preferences and adjust. When Karl rejects a survey method of monitoring, Laura does not push; there are other ways to get feedback.
- Focus on resources. Attend to strengths, resources and expectations, not just problems, right from the start.
- Do not be surprised at differing views of the relationship. Helper and client may see it differently, especially early on; look for cues throughout.
- Ups and downs are common. An upsetting insight or a sulk does not mean the relationship is in trouble. Horvath and colleagues see these variations as normal and, if attended to and resolved, linked with good outcomes.
- Expect and deal with client negativity. Therapy is hard work and frustrated clients may lash out. When Karl tells Laura she knows nothing about war, she does not take it personally but tries to learn from it.

The communication and relationship-building skills needed for all this are covered in Part II.
sections.simple: The working alliance is the collaborative partnership between client and helper, based on agreement about goals and tasks (Bordin). Helping is a two-person team effort; both share responsibility. Alliances emerge from good collaborative work, and helpers should track client needs, focus on strengths, and expect ups and downs and even client anger.
keyPoints: Norcross: the alliance is the quality and strength of client-therapist collaboration.
Bordin: collaboration based on agreement on goals and tasks.
Bachelor et al.: active, mutual and therapist-dependent collaboration (a third are dependent).
Helping is a two-person team effort; helpers do not 'cure' clients.
Six principles: alliances emerge, track needs, focus on resources, expect differing views, ups and downs, client negativity.

sections.heading: Getting Off to a Good Start
sections.simple: Research shows change often happens early, so a good start matters. DeFife and Hilsenroth suggest three things: build positive expectations, help clients take up an active, committed role, and set goals together. Keep it simple and do not overload the client with decisions.
keyPoints: Miller, Duncan et al.: early subjective improvement predicts positive outcome.
DeFife and Hilsenroth: three areas for a good start.
Build positive expectancies (framework, normalising, confidence, commitment).
Help clients become proactive, committed partners in the 'driver's seat'.
Emphasise collaborative goal formation; avoid overloading clients early.

sections.heading: Keeping the Client's Point of View and Preferences Center Stage
sections.detailed:
Bedi argued that researchers have paid too much attention to therapists' views of the relationship and neglected clients' views. Two questions follow: what kind of relationship does this client want (clients differ widely), and what does the therapist need to do to help the client become a collaborating partner?

Therapist attributes and techniques. Ackerman and Hilsenroth examined therapists' personal attributes and in-session activities that strengthen the alliance. The attributes were flexibility, honesty, respect, trustworthiness, confidence, warmth, interest and openness. Helpful techniques included exploration, reflection, noting past therapy success, accurate interpretation, facilitating the expression of feeling, and attending to the client's experience.

What clients value. Bedi's study found that clients appreciated the helping setting, the helper's self-presentation and body language, nonverbal gestures, emotional support and care, honesty, validation, guidance, challenge, the helper's education, the helper's respect for client self-responsibility, and well-run sessions. Duff and Bedi found that even small strengths-fostering behaviours, such as encouraging statements, positive comments about the client and greeting the client with a smile, may contribute disproportionately to alliance building. Bedi and Davis argue that helpers need training in client-focused behaviours, especially in programmes that overstress treatment methods.

Using this knowledge. For the helper this is background knowledge. What matters is tailoring what research shows to the individual client. Egan advises not to get lost in detail but to reflect on it and develop a natural personal style; Parts II and III give many examples of tailoring the relationship to the client.
sections.simple: Research has focused too much on what therapists think about the relationship and too little on what clients want. Studies show clients value warmth, honesty, support, validation and even small things like a smile. Helpers should use this as background and fit the relationship to each client.
keyPoints: Bedi: client views of the relationship have been neglected.
Key questions: what relationship does the client want, and how to make them a partner?
Ackerman and Hilsenroth: alliance-building attributes (flexibility, honesty, respect, warmth, etc.) and techniques.
Duff and Bedi: small strengths-fostering behaviours count a lot.
Tailor research knowledge to the individual client; develop a natural style.

sections.heading: The Relationship as a Forum for Relearning
sections.detailed:
Although helpers do not cure clients, the relationship itself can be therapeutic. In the working alliance it often acts as a forum or vehicle for social-emotional relearning (Mallinckrodt). Effective helpers model attitudes and behaviours that encourage clients to challenge and change their own.

Egan gives examples of what a client might implicitly say to themselves: since the helper obviously cares for and trusts me, perhaps I can care for and trust myself; the helper takes the risk of challenging me, and challenge done well is not so bad; I came terrified of relationships and now I am in a non-exploitative relationship I value.

Experimenting in sessions. Protected by the safety of the relationship, clients can try out new behaviours within the sessions: the shy person speaks up, the reclusive person opens up, the aggressive person backs off, and the overly sensitive person asks to be challenged.

Transfer to everyday life. Clients can then carry this learning into other social settings. A client may notice that the helper listens carefully and checks understanding even when disagreeing, and realise that doing the same would change her outside relationships. Another may see that the helper keeps self-control in the face of provocative behaviour without losing humanity, and want to do likewise.

Egan concludes that the relearning dynamic, even when subtle or covert, is often powerful: needed changes in attitudes, emotional expression and behaviour often occur within the sessions through the relationship itself.
sections.simple: The helping relationship can itself be a place where clients relearn how to relate. Clients learn from how the helper treats them, try new behaviours safely in sessions, and then use them in daily life.
keyPoints: Mallinckrodt: the relationship as a vehicle for social-emotional relearning.
Helpers model attitudes and behaviours clients can adopt.
Safety allows clients to experiment with new behaviours in sessions.
Learning transfers to relationships outside therapy.
Change in attitudes, emotional expression and behaviour can happen through the relationship itself.

sections.heading: Relationship Flexibility
sections.detailed:
Egan calls it a myth that one perfect relationship fits all clients. Clients have different needs, best met by different kinds of relationships and by adjusting within the same relationship. One client works best with a very warm helper, another with a more objective, businesslike one. Some clients fear intimacy, and lots of empathy and warmth from the outset may put them off; stronger interventions can follow once trust is established. Effective helpers use a mix of styles, skills and techniques tailored to each client (A. A. Lazarus; Mahrer) while remaining themselves.

Who takes the lead? Duncan, Miller and Sparks give an answer many see as radical. They argue that forty years of outcome research support privileging the client's role in change: clients, not therapists, make therapy work. Therapy should therefore be organised around clients' resources, perceptions, experiences and ideas, and therapists should take direction from clients, following their lead and adopting their language, worldview, goals and ideas about the problem. Egan notes this goes at least a step beyond Rogers's client-centred approach. The earlier phrase "no one right way to relate to a client" becomes "no one right way to put the client in the driver's seat". Thinking about the relationship continues to evolve.

Patience. A fully collaborative relationship may not appear at once. Keep doing the right things, remembering that what you think most important may not be what the client thinks. Karl says he keeps expecting to see Laura as a mother, teacher or nurse and himself as a child, student or patient, but does not feel that way; Laura reflects that it is taking time to understand what this relationship is, and Karl agrees it is new for him.

Ruptures. Breakdowns do happen, so helpers must know how to get back on track. Eubanks-Carter, Muran and Safran describe ways of handling challenges, misunderstandings, impasses, deterioration, stress and threats to the relationship, which they call ruptures, and show how ruptures can become opportunities for change and growth. Relationships are built through conversation and behaviour; the skills needed, including immediacy, are detailed in Part II.
sections.simple: No single type of relationship suits every client; helpers adjust warmth, style and technique to each person while staying themselves. Duncan, Miller and Sparks argue clients make therapy work, so helpers should follow their lead. Breakdowns, called ruptures, are normal and can become chances for growth.
keyPoints: One perfect relationship for all clients is a myth.
Tailor styles and techniques (A. A. Lazarus; Mahrer) while remaining yourself.
Duncan, Miller and Sparks: clients, not therapists, make therapy work.
This goes a step beyond Rogers's client-centred approach.
Eubanks-Carter, Muran and Safran: ruptures can become opportunities for growth.

sections.heading: The Values That Drive the Helping Relationship
sections.detailed:
One of the best ways to characterise a helping relationship is through the values that run through it. The relationship is the vehicle through which values come alive, and values, expressed concretely in working-alliance behaviours, play a critical part in helping. However, the uncertainties in the beliefs-values-norms-ethics-morality package described in Chapter 1 make this less clear-cut.

Professional codes. The ethical codes of the American Psychological Association, the American Counseling Association, the American Psychiatric Association and other bodies give a clear set of values and detailed norms for helper-client interaction. They reduce many uncertainties but do not remove them; ethical uncertainties and conflicts will always trouble helping. Egan presents values that many people, himself included, think should drive helping, but admits there is no universal agreement on the right package. In the end each helper must develop values that make sense to them and their clients and that comply with the codes and the law.

Espoused values and values-in-use. Drawing on Argyris (and Argyris and Schon), values can be seen as mental maps that define how to act in situations. People have values but do not always use them. So clients, like everyone, hold espoused values, which are like ideals, and values-in-use, the behavioural maps they actually use more or less consistently to make decisions and guide behaviour. There is often a gap between espoused values and action, in helper or client, which adds uncertainty to helping. Moreover, some values-in-use lead to life-limiting rather than life-enhancing outcomes.
sections.simple: Values are what drive the helping relationship, and the relationship is how those values show up in practice. Ethical codes help but do not remove all uncertainty. Argyris distinguishes values people say they hold (espoused) from values they actually act on (values-in-use).
keyPoints: The relationship is the vehicle through which values come alive.
Ethical codes (APA, ACA, American Psychiatric Association) reduce but do not remove uncertainty.
Helpers must build their own value set consistent with codes and law.
Argyris: values as mental maps; espoused values vs values-in-use.
Some values-in-use produce life-limiting outcomes.

sections.heading: Values as Tools of the Trade; Determining the Values Inherent to Successful Helping
sections.detailed:
Values as tools of the trade. Values-in-use are not just mental states but practical tools that guide decisions and give rise to client-enabling behaviour. Egan illustrates with a helper's inner reasoning about a difficult client with an arrogant, always-right attitude that distorts her decisions, poisons her relationships and keeps her stuck. The helper wants to give feedback or, better, invite her to challenge herself, without damaging the relationship. He values genuineness and openness, does not want to belittle her, but feels he owes it to her to help her see herself as others do, in the right way and at the right time. His values shape how he proceeds.

Helpers without working values are adrift. Those with no explicit values have an implicit, default set that may or may not serve the client. Reviewing the values behind your helping behaviour is therefore not optional.

Determining the values. Helping-related values cannot be handed over on a platter, much less forced on anyone. The chapter is meant to stimulate thinking: in the end only the beliefs, values and norms you have made your own will affect your helping behaviour. This does not mean inventing values unlike anyone else's; tradition matters in value formation, and helpers learn from the rich tradition of the helping professions.

Egan then names five major values from that tradition and translates them into norms:
1. Respect, the foundation value.
2. Empathy, the value that orients helpers in every interaction.
3. Proactive appreciation of diversity, which opens the helper to the world as it is.
4. Self-responsibility together with client empowerment.
5. A bias toward action, an outcome-focused value.

These are a starting point for reflection. Egan urges readers not to just swallow them but to analyse, reflect on and debate them and to build their own values package.
sections.simple: Values are practical tools that guide what a helper does in the moment. A helper without clear values falls back on unexamined default ones. Egan offers five values: respect, empathy, appreciation of diversity, self-responsibility/empowerment and a bias for action, but asks readers to think them through and make them their own.
keyPoints: Values-in-use are tools that guide decisions and client-enabling behaviour.
Helpers without explicit values work from an implicit 'default' set.
Values cannot be imposed; only owned values affect behaviour.
Tradition of the helping professions informs value formation.
Five values: respect (foundation), empathy (orientation), diversity, self-responsibility/empowerment, bias for action (outcome).

sections.heading: Respect as the Foundation Value; Behaviors Showing Disrespect
sections.detailed:
Respect for clients is the foundation of all helping interventions. Like most fundamental concepts it resists definition. The word comes from a Latin root involving 'seeing' or 'viewing', and respect is indeed a particular way of viewing oneself and others. But to make a difference it cannot stay an attitude; it has to show in behaviour. Ideally helpers and clients "matter to one another" (Rayle).

Carl Rogers recognised the importance of respect early, calling it positive regard and adding nonpossessive warmth toward and affirmation of the client. Later research (Farber and Doolin) links these behaviours to successful outcomes. Egan derives norms from the interaction between a belief in the dignity of the person and the value of respect. First, behaviours to avoid.

Do no harm. This is the first rule of the physician and of the helper (Lilienfeld; Rhule). Yet some helpers do harm because they are unprincipled or incompetent. Helping is not neutral; it works for better or for worse. In a world where child abuse, wife battering and exploitation of workers are more common than we like to think, helpers must take a non-manipulative, non-exploitative approach.

Do not rush to judgement. Helpers are not there to judge clients or impose their values, but to help clients identify, explore, review and challenge the consequences of the values they hold. Egan's example: a client says arrogantly that he says what he wants when he wants and others' dislike is their problem, because his first duty is to himself. An irritated helper might reply judgementally that the client has just named the core of his problem and ask how he expects to get along with such a self-centred philosophy. A second counsellor instead reflects that being himself is a top priority and total frankness is part of that. The first rushes to judgement; the second neither judges nor condones, but tries to understand and show understanding, even though she sees the client might later benefit from exploring the unintended consequences of his philosophy.
sections.simple: Respect is the base on which all helping rests; it means seeing clients in a certain way and acting on it. Rogers called it positive regard. Showing disrespect includes doing harm and rushing to judge clients instead of understanding them.
keyPoints: Respect is the foundation of all helping interventions.
Latin root: 'seeing' or 'viewing'; must go beyond attitude into behaviour.
Rogers: positive regard plus nonpossessive warmth; Farber and Doolin link it to outcomes.
Do no harm: helping is 'for better or for worse'.
Do not rush to judgement: understand without judging or condoning.

sections.heading: Behaviors Showing Respect
sections.detailed:
Egan lists behaviours through which helpers show respect.

Become competent and committed. Master the helping model you use and become skilled in the problem-management and opportunity-development framework and its skills. There is no place for the "caring incompetent". Egan regrets that not every graduate of a training programme is competent or grows in competence over a career.

Be genuine. Gelso and others (Kolden and colleagues) distinguish the real relationship from the alliance. Gelso defines the real relationship as the personal relationship between people, reflected in how genuine each is with the other and how far each perceives the other in ways that fit the other. So the relationship is real to the extent it is empathic and not phony. Pretending to like someone you do not is phony, and phoniness is incompatible with respect. Another form of phoniness is overstressing your professional role. With a client, the helper is a helper, catalyst, encourager and collaborator, not primarily a member of a profession, an expert or the one with answers. The client's success is the helper's success; you are competent to the degree the client improves.

Make it clear that you are 'for' the client. Your manner should convey that you care in a down-to-earth, non-sentimental way, as if saying working with the client is worth your time and energy. Respect is both gracious and tough-minded. Being for the client is not taking the client's side or being their advocate; it means taking their views seriously even when they need challenge. Respect often involves helping clients place demands on themselves; this tough love does not rule out appropriate warmth.

Assume the client's goodwill. Assume clients want to live more effectively until proved otherwise. Reluctance and resistance, especially in involuntary clients, are not necessarily signs of ill will; respect means entering the client's world to understand the reluctance and helping them work through it.

Keep the client's agenda in focus. Helpers should pursue the client's agenda, not their own. Three helpers lost clients through failing at this: one became preoccupied with his theories of depression rather than the client's painful episodes; another dismissed a client's grief over a dead pet as trivial, and the client attempted suicide, the loss being the last straw in a downward spiral; a third, a white male counsellor proud of his multicultural focus, lost a Hispanic client who said, perhaps unfairly, that he was more interested in Anglo-Hispanic politics than in her.
sections.simple: Respect shows in action: being competent and committed, being genuine rather than phony or hiding behind a professional role, being clearly 'for' the client, assuming goodwill, and following the client's agenda rather than your own.
keyPoints: Become competent and committed; no room for the 'caring incompetent'.
Be genuine: Gelso's 'real relationship'; phoniness, including overplaying the professional role, is disrespectful.
Be 'for' the client: gracious and tough-minded, not the same as taking sides.
Assume goodwill; reluctance is not proof of ill will.
Keep the client's agenda in focus (three cautionary cases).

sections.heading: Empathy as the Primary Orientation Value
sections.detailed:
Empathy is a key way of showing respect. Egan defines it as the ability to understand the client from the client's point of view and, when appropriate, to communicate that understanding. Put simply, it means understanding and feeling for another person's mental states and emotions, and, Egan adds, understanding how the person's context shapes their thinking and feeling. The empathic person experiences the other in context.

Although rich, empathy has been a confusing concept. The literature is vast, with philosophers, psychologists, theoreticians and practitioners all contributing (Batson, Coplan and Goldie, Decety, Elliott and colleagues, and others), and definitions differ:
- Empathy as a personality trait: a disposition to feel what others feel or understand them from the inside. On this view some people are naturally more empathic than others.
- Empathy as a situation-specific state of feeling for and understanding another's experiences. The implication is that helpers can learn to bring about this state because it is useful in counselling.
- Empathy as a process with stages, building on the state view. Barrett-Lennard identified three phases: empathic resonance, expressed empathy and received empathy. Carl Rogers spoke of sensing the client's inner world and communicating that sensing.

Egan simplifies matters for helpers: this chapter treats empathy as a basic value that informs and drives all helping behaviour, while Chapter 4 treats empathy as a communication skill.
sections.simple: Empathy means understanding clients from their point of view, including their feelings and life context, and communicating that understanding when helpful. It has been described as a trait, a state, or a process with stages. Here Egan treats it as a value that guides all helping.
keyPoints: Empathy: understanding the client from their point of view and communicating it when appropriate.
Includes understanding how context shapes thinking and feeling.
Defined variously as trait, situation-specific state, or staged process.
Barrett-Lennard: empathic resonance, expressed empathy, received empathy.
Chapter 2: empathy as a value; Chapter 4: empathy as a skill.

sections.heading: A Brief Overview of Empathy
sections.detailed:
All theoreticians, researchers and practitioners agree empathy matters in everyday life and in helping. Egan then looks at several facets.

Is empathy even possible? Can a helper understand a very different client: a 'normal' person someone with bipolar disorder, or a Hispanic male counsellor a middle-class female Iranian-American client? The practical answer is yes (Hatcher and colleagues). Clients working with helpers who hold empathy as a value and have the communication skills of Part II can feel understood. The underlying philosophical question is another matter.

A rich concept, perhaps too rich for a scientist. Several authors treat empathy as a value and describe the behaviours that flow from it, sometimes almost lyrically. Kohut described empathy as an accepting, confirming and understanding human echo, a psychological nutrient without which human life could not be sustained. Covey named empathic communication one of the seven habits of highly effective people, saying it gives others psychological air to breathe more freely in relationships. Goleman put empathy at the heart of emotional intelligence: it is a person's social radar for sensing others' feelings and perspectives and taking an active interest in their concerns.

The importance of empathy early in life. Research commissioned by the WAVE Trust, an international charity working on the root causes of violence, concluded that empathy is the single greatest inhibitor of a propensity to violence, and that empathy fails to develop when parents or prime carers fail to attune to their infants (Hosking and Walsh). They defined empathy as others' observed experiences affecting our thoughts and feelings in a caring way, which involves stepping outside oneself emotionally and temporarily suspending one's own perspective to take another's. To attune to a child means trying to respond to the child's needs, especially emotional ones, so the child feels understood, cared for and valued.

Children should also learn to express empathy. Kennedy argues that unless children both experience and express empathy, they risk becoming self-centred, aggressive and cruel and unable to feel or show remorse, a quasi-sociopathic style. This happens when parents are physically or emotionally unavailable, when they are overindulgent, and when children are exposed to violent media. Kennedy urges parents to talk about others' emotions, model empathic communication, teach children to make amends, expose them to the less fortunate, let them feel useful unhappiness such as the frustration of not getting their way, and shield them from violent media.
sections.simple: Empathy across differences is possible in practice: clients can feel understood. Writers like Kohut, Covey and Goleman describe empathy in glowing terms. Research shows empathy develops when carers attune to infants and protects against violence, and children also need to learn to show empathy.
keyPoints: Hatcher et al.: practically, empathy across differences is possible.
Kohut: empathy as a psychological nutrient; Covey: 'psychological air'; Goleman: 'social radar' in emotional intelligence.
WAVE Trust (Hosking and Walsh): empathy is the greatest inhibitor of violence; needs parental attunement.
Attunement: responding to a child's emotional needs so they feel understood and valued.
Kennedy: children must experience and express empathy; parental guidelines.

sections.heading: Empathy as a Two-Way Street
sections.detailed:
Pedersen, Crethar and Carlson show that helpers can become more competent by going beyond the traditional view of one individual helper trying to understand one individual client. At its best, empathy is relationship-oriented. Zaki, Bolger and Ochsner showed that empathic accuracy depends on how both people in a conversation communicate. Pedersen and colleagues explore how cultural similarities and differences shape counselling relationships and argue helpers should focus less on individuals and more on relationships.

Janet Clark has reconceptualised empathy in a similar way. Like Pedersen, she defines culture very broadly, including the traits and characteristics that make individuals different. She uses ethnographic concepts to focus on the individual client's unique frame of reference rather than that of a cultural group. She contrasts traditional one-way, individualistic empathy with diversity-oriented, two-way relationship empathy, which Pedersen calls "inclusive cultural empathy". Her principles are:
- The client's reality is knowable, but the helper's understanding is always partial and fallible.
- Helpers must attune not only to underlying mental states and feelings but also to the cultural meaning of the client's words.
- Relationship empathy is not only person-centred; it includes the key contexts of the client's life.
- The client's complex sociopolitical environment and status, their social location, is often a key part of context.
- Regarding the client's cultural uniqueness, the helper is a learner, not an expert.
- The client's inductive understandings of self and world matter more than the helper's deductive understandings drawn from theory, research and practice.
- Empathy is not offered one-way by the helper but produced mutually through dialogue.
- Self-awareness of cultural bias is not enough; ongoing self-reflexivity about ideas, fears, mistakes, confusion, breakthroughs and obstacles arising in sessions is essential.
sections.simple: Empathy works best as something built between two people, not just something a helper does to a client. Clark and Pedersen describe 'inclusive cultural empathy', in which the helper is a learner about the client's culture and understanding is created through dialogue.
keyPoints: Pedersen, Crethar and Carlson: empathy at its best is relationship-oriented.
Zaki, Bolger and Ochsner: empathic accuracy depends on how both parties communicate.
Janet Clark: two-way relationship empathy vs one-way individualistic empathy.
Pedersen's term: 'inclusive cultural empathy'.
Helper as learner; empathy mutually produced; continuous self-reflexivity; attention to social location.

sections.heading: Empathy as Radical Commitment
sections.detailed:
As a value, empathy is a radical commitment by helpers to understand clients as fully as possible in three ways.

1. Understanding the client's point of view. A commitment to understand each client from their own point of view, together with the feelings surrounding it, and to communicate this understanding whenever it seems helpful.

2. Understanding the client in context. A commitment to understand people in and through the context of their lives. The social settings, large and small, in which they have developed and currently live provide routes to understanding.

3. Understanding the gap between point of view and reality. A commitment to understand the dissonance between the client's view and reality. Giving feedback on this third kind of empathy is sensitive and is discussed in Part II.

Empathy is active, not passive. Empathic helpers respectfully communicate these kinds of understanding and take an active interest in clients' concerns. Respectful empathy is especially important with clients who differ from the helper personally, socially or culturally (Wang and colleagues). Chapter 4 will show that communicating empathy is also one of the best ways of keeping clients in the driver's seat.
sections.simple: Empathy as a value is a strong commitment to understand clients fully: their point of view and feelings, their life context, and the gap between how they see things and how things are. It is active, not passive, and especially important with clients who are different from you.
keyPoints: Three commitments: client's point of view, client in context, dissonance between view and reality.
Communicate understanding whenever helpful.
Feedback on the third type is sensitive (Part II).
Empathy is active, not passive.
Especially important with clients who differ from the helper (Wang et al.); keeps clients in the driver's seat.

sections.heading: Proactive Appreciation of Diversity
sections.detailed:
Dealing knowledgeably and sensitively with diversity (Muran), including the particular form called multiculturalism, is part of respect and empathy and is linked to client empowerment. Egan gives it special attention because of its own importance and because of society's current emphasis on diversity. The most important feature of this focus is that it highlights client factors as the essential ingredient of successful therapy. In Egan's words, it is not about the countless forms of diversity, nor about culture; it is about clients.

The literature has exploded (Bernal and Domenech Rodriguez, Hays, Lewis and colleagues, Ponterotto and colleagues, and others). An internet bookseller search gave over 16,000 entries, a dictionary of multicultural psychology (L. E. Hall) runs over 170 pages, and whole journal issues are devoted to it, so Egan hesitates to recommend particular readings.

Upsides. The flood of literature forces helpers to examine their blind spots about diversity, including ethnic and cultural diversity, and to look more deeply at the world. There is also evidence that exposure to multiple cultures can itself enhance creativity (Leung, Maddux, Galinsky and Chiu); Egan adds that this probably applies to all forms of diversity.

Downsides. Multiculturalism risks becoming a fad that spawns an industry and draws attention away from individual clients' needs. Putnam found a short-term minus: the more diverse a community, the less its inhabitants trust anyone, from neighbours to the mayor, and Egan thinks this is probably true at the individual level too. In the long term diversity can be enriching, but not automatically. Mere contact is not enough (Dixon, Durrheim and Tredoux); communities and individuals must work at it.
sections.simple: Appreciating diversity is part of respect and empathy, and its real point is the individual client, not culture as such. The huge literature helps expose blind spots and diversity can boost creativity, but it can become a fad, and Putnam found diverse communities show less trust in the short term.
keyPoints: Diversity work is part of respect and empathy, linked to empowerment.
Its key message: client factors are the essential ingredient; 'it's about clients'.
Upsides: exposes blind spots; multicultural exposure can enhance creativity (Leung et al.).
Downsides: risk of a fad/industry; Putnam: more diversity, less trust (short term).
Mere contact is not enough (Dixon et al.); diversity must be worked at.

sections.heading: Culture, Personal Culture, and Values
sections.detailed:
Since culture is the form of diversity that gets most attention, helpers need to understand the term. Bronfenbrenner called culture the largest and most controlling of systems at individual and societal levels. There are many definitions, but helpers need practical ones. Values are central to culture, but culture is more than values. Egan's fuller notion: shared beliefs and assumptions interact with shared values to produce shared norms, which drive shared patterns of behaviour. Culture usually applies to societies, institutions, companies, professions, groups and families, but counsellors work with individuals and small groups, so Egan applies the framework to the individual, using Isaiah, a client with PTSD after gang violence and a brutal attack:
- Assumptions and beliefs: over life, people develop beliefs about themselves, others and the world. Isaiah believes the world is heartless.
- Values: what people prize, picked up along life's path. Isaiah prizes personal security.
- Norms: beliefs interacting with values generate internal dos and don'ts. Isaiah's norm: do not trust people or you will get hurt.
- Patterns of behaviour: norms drive internal and external behaviour patterns, the bottom line of personal culture, 'the way I live my life'. Isaiah stays on defensive alert, takes no chances with people and tends to be a loner.

Personal cultures are not formed in a vacuum; group memberships strongly shape beliefs, values and norms. Yet individuals personalise them, tailoring them in different ways (Massimini and Delle Fave). Individuals are not cultural carbon copies, and people from the same social culture can differ widely in personal culture. Effective helpers understand both a client's cultural background and personal culture. Isaiah shares many traits of his family, ethnic group, neighbourhood, school and class, but his mix is unique.

A popular definition of group culture is 'the way we do things here'; for an individual client it becomes 'the way I choose to live my life', and for a helper 'the way I do helping'. The helper's social-personal-professional culture inevitably interacts with the client's, for better or worse.

Egan illustrates with Sue Smith, a Midwestern American, married to Patrick Lee, an immigrant from Singapore, seeing marriage counsellor Antonio Ochoa, a Hispanic-American son of immigrants. Since many clients come with relationship difficulties, understanding different approaches to relationships matters. Guisinger and Blatt note that Western psychologies have favoured self-development (autonomy, independence, identity) over interpersonal relatedness, whereas women, many minority groups and non-Western societies have emphasised relatedness; both are essential for maturity. Sue is focused on autonomy and her identity as a successful working woman; Patrick runs a small web business. Helping them find the right balance requires understanding what 'right balance' means in each culture and each personal culture; Antonio must put Clark's principles into practice. When cultural values clash (Knapp and VandeCreek), which prevails? Multiculturalism solves some problems and raises others.
sections.simple: Culture is shared beliefs and values producing shared norms and behaviour patterns. Applied to a person, this becomes 'personal culture': the way I live my life. People are shaped by their groups but are never carbon copies, so helpers must understand both the cultural background and the unique personal culture of each client.
keyPoints: Bronfenbrenner: culture is the largest and most controlling of systems.
Culture: beliefs/assumptions + values -> norms -> patterns of behaviour.
Personal culture ('the way I live my life'), illustrated by Isaiah.
Individuals personalise culture (Massimini and Delle Fave); not carbon copies.
Guisinger and Blatt: self-development vs relatedness; case of Sue, Patrick and Antonio.

sections.heading: Helper Competencies Related to Client Diversity
sections.detailed:
Diversity competence is the knowledge and skill needed to relate to and communicate effectively with people who differ from us in any significant way. Cross-cultural competence gets most attention (Constantine and Sue and others), but other forms of diversity are just as important. Many competency lists, hefty handbooks (Pope-Davis and colleagues) and countless studies exist. Day describes multicultural counselling competence as awareness of one's own culture, biases and values; knowledge of social and cultural influences on individuals; and skills for applying this knowledge in counselling. Still, there is no universal agreement on the right package (Kia 'I Kitaoka). Egan offers broad guidelines.

Understand and appreciate diversity. Clients share humanity but differ in many ways: abilities, accent, age, attractiveness, colour, developmental stage, disability, economic status, education, ethnicity, fitness, gender, group culture, health, national origin, occupation, personal culture, personality, politics, problem type, religion, sexual orientation and social status. Hays offers the ADDRESSING framework: Age, Developmental and acquired Disabilities, Religion, Ethnicity, Socioeconomic status, Sexual orientation, Indigenous heritage and Gender, to help therapists recognise, understand and address diversity and multiculturalism in a multidimensional way. Since people differ in hundreds of ways, helpers must understand clients and problems contextually: a life-threatening illness means different things at 20 and 80; a homeless former graduate student with a drug history differs from a drifter who hates shelters. Helpers can learn a lot about the populations they serve, such as lifespan tasks or the needs of the elderly, but cannot know everything about every population or syndrome. Egan asks how a highly educated African American female psychologist could fully understand a poor, homeless, middle-aged lapsed-Catholic man of Mexican and Polish parentage, and indeed how anyone can fully understand anyone. Pushed too far, diversity principles would make helping impossible.

Challenge your diversity blind spots. Because helpers differ from clients, they risk blind spots that cause inept interventions; for example, an attractive extroverted helper may misjudge the social flexibility and self-esteem of an unattractive introverted client. Counsellors should become aware of their own cultural values and biases, try to understand clients' worldviews, and take special care with the key ways they differ from clients.

Tailor interventions in a diversity-sensitive way. Understanding and self-knowledge must become appropriate interventions. How a Hispanic helper challenges a Hispanic client may not suit a white client, and vice versa; how a younger helper self-discloses to a young client may not suit an older one. Intimate self-disclosure may be easier for someone from North American culture than from, say, Asian or British culture. A middle-class helper should check assumptions about poverty, and with a disabled client should not feel sorry but try to see the world from their perspective. Personal cultures within the same social culture differ: Egan bristles at 'I know you Irish'. A client from a disclosure-friendly culture may still be terrified of disclosure; one gay client may be proud of his identity and another ashamed. Check all group assumptions at the door.

Work with individuals. The more helpers understand broad characteristics of populations, the better they can adapt the process to individuals; but helpers work with individuals, not groups. Satel says psychotherapy cannot be about celebrating racial diversity because it is about individuals and their infinite complexity. Category traits can destroy understanding as well as aid it. Focus on the diversity factors relevant to this client and this problem, or you will get lost in the weeds and lose the client. There are no homogeneous groups; social psychology shows as many or more differences within groups as between them (Weinrach and Thomas). Even a conversation between identical twins is a cross-cultural event (Brenner). Valuing diversity is not the same as a splintered society where group membership outranks humanity, and valuing individuality is not a 'society of one'. Egan's example is Sean, 26: bright, gay, Hispanic, poorly educated, underemployed, feeling defeated and trapped. Understand him in any way you can, but work with Sean.
sections.simple: Diversity competence is the knowledge and skill to work with people who differ from us in any way. Helpers should understand diversity (e.g. Hays's ADDRESSING framework), challenge their own blind spots, adapt interventions sensitively, and above all treat each client as a unique individual rather than a member of a group.
keyPoints: Diversity competence: knowledge and skills for relating to anyone significantly different.
Day: awareness, knowledge and skills; no universal agreement on the package.
Hays's ADDRESSING framework; understand clients contextually.
Challenge blind spots and tailor interventions; check group assumptions at the door.
Work with individuals: more variation within than between groups (Weinrach and Thomas); Satel; case of Sean.

sections.heading: Specific Multicultural Competencies
sections.detailed:
Cultural Competence Continuum. The National Center for Cultural Competence at Georgetown University adapted, from a monograph by Cross and colleagues, a framework called the Cultural Competence Continuum with six stages: cultural destructiveness, cultural incapacity, cultural blindness, cultural pre-competence, cultural competence and cultural proficiency. Cultural competence includes acceptance and respect for difference, continuing self-assessment, careful attention to the dynamics of difference, continuous expansion of knowledge and resources, and adapting services to meet diverse needs. Egan likes that it uses the language of diversity rather than the narrower language of culture.

Egan's adapted list. Egan adapts a list by Hansen, Pepitone-Arreola-Rockwell and Greene, openly adding his own bias that diversity, especially personal culture, is the key concept, with culture one important factor among many. The counsellor must engage each client's personal culture. The competencies are:
- Be aware of your own personal culture and heritage and how you may come across to people who differ from you.
- Be aware of your personal-culture biases toward other individuals and groups.
- Be aware of ways you are similar to and different from each client; both can help or hinder.
- Understand the values, beliefs and worldviews of the groups and individuals you work with.
- Understand how all kinds of diversity contribute to each client's makeup.
- Be aware of how sociopolitical influences such as poverty, oppression, stereotyping, stigma, discrimination, prejudice and marginalisation may have affected clients; any form of diversity, such as age, education or disability, can be a target.
- Realise that mainstream Western theories, research methods, diagnoses, assessments and practices may not fit other cultures, or even all Westerners, without adaptation.
- Know the basics of family structure and gender roles in client groups, remembering within-culture differences.
- Understand how different cultures view and handle illness, including mental illness, and help-seeking.
- Build rapport and convey empathy in culturally sensitive ways, to individuals, not cultures; do not assume people from your own culture are alike.
- Recognise differences in interaction style and language, including nonverbal communication.
- When clients tell their stories, distinguish culture-specific issues from universal human experience; problems with parents are nearly universal (Egan quotes a Jacques Brel line asking which child is without complaint), but their specific twists are often culturally conditioned.
- Design non-biased treatment plans that factor in cultural and personal-culture variables.
- Raise and explore differences between yourself and clients when appropriate; ultimately the interaction is personal culture to personal culture.
- Assess your own cross-cultural and personal-culture competence and keep improving.

Keep it simple. Work with clients as they are, without apologising for who you are. Adding up all cultural-competence principles is dizzying; Collins, Arthur and Wong-Wylie's 'cultural audit' of 13 steps and over 60 questions is, for Egan, a step too far. Stuart notes it is easy to endorse culturally sensitive practice but much harder to achieve it, and writes about avoiding over- or under-valuing cultural-competence behaviours. No one holds a 'pure' culture: everyone belongs to multiple groups (nation, region, gender, religion, age cohort, occupation) whose influences may agree or conflict, and each person interprets them, so everyone is a unique blend. It is never safe to infer someone's cultural orientation from a group they are thought to belong to. Egan praises Stuart's 12 practical suggestions as an excellent starting point that neither overstates nor understates culture and stresses diversity beyond culture.
sections.simple: The Cultural Competence Continuum runs through six stages from cultural destructiveness to cultural proficiency. Egan lists practical competencies like knowing your own culture and biases, understanding clients' worldviews and sociopolitical pressures, and adapting Western methods. He warns against overcomplicating it: everyone is a unique blend, so never assume a person's views from their group.
keyPoints: Cultural Competence Continuum (Cross et al.): destructiveness, incapacity, blindness, pre-competence, competence, proficiency.
Egan adapts Hansen et al.'s list with his bias toward personal culture.
Self-awareness, knowledge of worldviews, sociopolitical influences, limits of Western methods.
Distinguish culture-specific from universal issues; non-biased treatment plans.
Stuart: no one has a 'pure' culture; never infer orientation from group membership; cultural audit is 'a step too far'.

sections.heading: Self-Responsibility as an Empowerment-Focused Value
sections.detailed:
Egan opens with Robert Zoellick, president of the World Bank, who, reviewing global problems, rejected labels like the Age of Reversal, Intolerance or Decline for the first half of the 21st century and chose 'the Age of Responsibility'.

Client responsibility assumes the client has the power to do what is right for self and others. Two goals of helping from Chapter 1, helping clients develop a problem-management and opportunity-development approach to life and a preference for prevention over cure, are both empowerment skills.

However, helpers do not empower clients. Rather, they help clients discover, acquire, develop and use the power they already have for constructive change; that is, they help clients identify, develop and use resources that make them more effective agents of change both in sessions and in everyday life (Strong, Yoder and Corcoran).

The opposite of empowerment is dependency (Abramson and colleagues; Bornstein and Bowen), deference (Rennie) and oppression (McWhirter). Because clients often experience helpers as relatively powerful, and because even the most egalitarian, client-centred helpers influence clients, helpers must come to terms with social influence in helping.
sections.simple: Self-responsibility means clients have the power to do what is right for themselves and others. Helpers do not hand out power; they help clients find and use the power they already have. The opposite is dependency, deference and oppression, so helpers must handle their influence carefully.
keyPoints: Zoellick: 'the Age of Responsibility'.
Client responsibility assumes the client can do what is right for self and others.
Helpers do not empower; they help clients discover and use their own power.
Opposites of empowerment: dependency, deference, oppression.
Helpers inevitably influence clients, so social influence must be faced.

sections.heading: Helping as a Social-Influence Process
sections.detailed:
People influence one another constantly. E. R. Smith and Mackie count influence among eight basic principles for understanding behaviour, and Crano calls social-influence research the defining hallmark of social psychology. Parents, children, teachers, students, bosses, subordinates and team members all influence one another.

Rashotte distinguishes social influence from power plays: social influence is change in a person's thoughts, feelings, attitudes or behaviour that results from interaction with another person or group, distinct from conformity, power and authority; people make real changes through interaction with others seen as similar, desirable or expert. Clients dislike influence they see as power because power often leads to manipulation and oppression (McCarthy and Frieze).

Strong's influential article, 'Counseling: An Interpersonal Influence Process', triggered much research on helping as social influence. Corrigan and associates' extensive 1980 review opened by observing that virtually all relationships involve attempts at influence and ended, after forty pages, with the blunt conclusion that counsellors are influential, leaving open how and for what purpose. Perrin and colleagues suggest the recent emphasis on diversity and multiculturalism has reduced helpers' tendency to over-influence clients, de-emphasising top-down influence in favour of an interactive, reciprocal, collegial process.

Egan's point: influence pervades helping, but helpers can influence clients without robbing them of self-responsibility, and can work so clients are empowered rather than oppressed in sessions and in daily life. A growing social-justice literature raises the theme of power imbalance, with the helper 'one up', though Zur has challenged this. The properly empowered client, whose resources for self-regulation and improvement are recognised, still faces the challenge of exercising self-responsibility.

A continuum of influence. Imagine a line from 'directing clients' lives' to 'leaving clients completely to their own devices'. Thaler and Sunstein argue the latter is impossible: in many situations someone must make choices that affect others, nudging is unavoidable, and nudges shape choices whether intended or not; helping is such a situation. Somewhere in between lies 'helping clients make their own decisions and act on them', where most helper influence falls. Stopping a client from jumping off a bridge is at the controlling end; simply accepting a client's decision to delay facing a troubled relationship because they are 'not ready' is toward the other end. Hare-Mustin and Marecek note the tension between clients' right to run their own lives and the therapist's obligation to help them live more effectively.
sections.simple: Helping always involves influence, just like any relationship. Research (Strong; Corrigan) shows counsellors are influential. The goal is to influence clients in a way that empowers them rather than controlling them, somewhere between directing their lives and leaving them completely alone.
keyPoints: Rashotte: social influence is change through interaction, distinct from conformity, power and authority.
Strong: counselling as an interpersonal influence process; Corrigan et al.: 'counselors are influential'.
Perrin et al.: diversity focus shifted influence toward reciprocal, collegial forms.
Helpers can influence without robbing clients of self-responsibility.
Continuum from directing to leaving alone; Thaler and Sunstein: nudging is unavoidable; Hare-Mustin and Marecek's tension.

sections.heading: Norms for Empowerment and Self-Responsibility
sections.detailed:
Helpers do not self-righteously empower clients; that would be patronising. Freire warned against making helping another form of oppression for the oppressed. Effective counsellors help clients discover, develop and use their untapped power. Egan gives empowerment norms, some adapted from Farrelly and Brandsma.

Start with the premise that clients can change if they choose. Clients have more resources than they or their helpers assume. These may be blocked or unused; the counsellor helps identify, free and cultivate them, and helps clients assess them realistically so aspirations do not outstrip resources.

Do not see clients as victims. Even if victimised by institutions or people, clients are not helpless. The cult of victimhood is growing too fast. Where circumstances limit freedom, as with an abused spouse unable to leave, work with the freedom that remains.

Do not be fooled by appearances. A trainer dismissed a reserved, self-deprecating trainee as 'more like a client than a trainee'; she became one of the programme's best students and was hired by a prestigious mental-health centre.

Share the helping process with clients. Explicit and implicit contracts govern many relationships, such as marriage and friendship. In collaborative helping both parties must know their responsibilities. Egan prefers 'working charter' to 'contract', avoiding legal overtones. It should cover: (1) the nature and goals of helping; (2) an overview of the approach and techniques; (3) the flexibility built in; (4) how the process helps clients reach goals; (5) relevant information about the helper; (6) how the relationship is structured and each party's responsibilities; (7) the values driving helping; and (8) procedural issues, such as where and how long sessions are and limits like contact between sessions. Manthei and Miller wrote a practical book on charters for clients, and charters seem to work even with the seriously mentally ill (Heinssen, Levendusky and Hunter). Helping should not be a black box; clients have a right to know what they are getting into. Helpers can explain, use a simple pamphlet, or, like Reis and Brown, a short video, sharing details over several sessions without overwhelming distressed clients. Clients should be told as much as they can reasonably assimilate.

Help clients see sessions as work sessions. Sessions explore the need for change, decide what change is needed, create programmes of change, run change 'pilot projects' and deal with obstacles. This is work, sometimes agonising, sometimes exhilarating. Building a work ethic in clients may be one of the helper's toughest challenges; some helpers cancel sessions until the client is ready to work, though helping clients find incentives is less dramatic.

Become a coach or consultant. Helpers can act as coaches or expert consultants (Mee-Lee, McLellan and Miller). Business consultants listen, observe, collect data, teach, support, challenge, advise and even advocate, but managers keep responsibility for decisions. Coaching is collaborative influence that does not rob managers, or clients, of their responsibilities. The best clients learn to use their helpers to add value.

Accept helping as a natural, two-way influence process. Tyler, Pargament and Gatz proposed the 'resource collaborator role'. Seeing both parties as people with defects, they stressed give-and-take: either can initiate helping, both have equal status in defining the relationship, originating actions and evaluating outcomes, and ideally both change. Egan's example: Wei-Lian corrects his counsellor Timothy, who reflects that Wei-Lian dislikes his father forcing opinions on him; Wei-Lian replies that he must respect his father and listen to his wisdom. Timothy realises he has been using his own cultural assumptions and says he needs to be more of a learner.

Focus on learning instead of helping. Helping is better seen as a learning process than an education process: sessions and the time between involve learning, unlearning and relearning. Howell said learning is incorporated into living to the extent that viable options are increased. Successful collaboration gives clients more degrees of freedom as they open up and act on options.

Do not see clients as overly fragile. Neither pampering nor brutalising helps. Helpers who constantly see clients as fragile may be protecting themselves. Driscoll noted many helpers do little more than listen early on. Clients' natural deference (Rennie), including fear of criticising the therapist, trying to understand the therapist's frame of reference, meeting perceived expectations and showing indebtedness, and fear of irretrievable error, can mislead helpers; it does not mean fragility. Driscoll urged intervening more from the start, by reasonably challenging clients' thinking and action and getting them to say what they want.

Cultural differences. Lin found Taiwanese university students tend to see help-seeking as weakness or shame, prefer informal help, seek help only when things are serious, and avoid strangers, holding beliefs like 'God helps people who help themselves'. This self-reliance differs greatly from Western individualism such as in Australia and the US. In the end, what matters is this client's approach to self-responsibility.
sections.simple: Helpers should not 'empower' clients patronisingly but help them use their own power. Norms include believing clients can change, not treating them as victims or as fragile, sharing the process through a working charter, treating sessions as work, acting like a coach, accepting two-way influence and focusing on learning.
keyPoints: Freire: helping must not become another form of oppression.
Clients can change if they choose; do not see them as victims or overly fragile; do not be fooled by appearances.
Working charter with eight elements; helping should not be a 'black box'.
Sessions as work sessions; helper as coach/consultant (Mee-Lee et al.); resource collaborator role (Tyler, Pargament and Gatz).
Learning focus (Howell); client deference (Rennie); Driscoll: intervene early; Lin: Taiwanese students' self-reliance.

sections.heading: Conscientiousness
sections.detailed:
The growing literature on conscientiousness (Bogg and Roberts; Friedman and Martin; Hill and colleagues; B. W. Roberts, Walton and Bogg) is another rich source for understanding and developing self-responsibility.

Bogg and Roberts define conscientiousness as individual differences in the propensity to follow socially prescribed norms for impulse control, to be task- and goal-oriented, to be planful, to delay gratification and to follow norms and rules.

Some might read this as a description of a dull person, while others link it to social-emotional intelligence and maturity.

Origins are uncertain. We do not know whether conscientiousness as a trait is genetically or neurologically determined, a product of personal and social development, or something acquired through choice and effort. Egan's own reading suggests it is probably some of each.

But the research is consistent that conscientious people live longer and healthier lives, and Egan expects future research to show further personal and social benefits. For helpers, conscientiousness offers a way of thinking about the qualities clients need in order to take charge of their lives.
sections.simple: Conscientiousness is the tendency to control impulses, be goal-oriented, plan, delay gratification and follow rules. Research shows conscientious people live longer, healthier lives. It may come from genes, development, choice, or probably all three.
keyPoints: Conscientiousness is a source for understanding self-responsibility.
Bogg and Roberts: impulse control, task/goal orientation, planfulness, delayed gratification, rule-following.
Seen by some as dull, by others as maturity and social-emotional intelligence.
Origins: genetic, developmental or chosen; probably some of each.
Conscientious people live longer and healthier lives.

sections.heading: Self-Responsibility, Self-Regulation, Self-Control
sections.detailed:
Self-regulation or self-control (Hoyle) is a key component of self-responsibility, though Egan wonders how much of it shows in everyday life. Baumeister and colleagues define self-regulation as a highly adaptive, distinctively human trait that lets people override and alter their responses, including changing themselves to meet social and other standards.

Despite its value, many people, especially children, seem to have little self-control, which can be maddening. In a controversial book, Druckerman suggests French children behave better than American children because French parents indulge them less. Self-indulgence, or being indulged, often leads to trouble, and when it becomes part of a culture, society is in trouble.

Our own lapses in self-control get us into trouble too, so it is unsurprising that poor self-regulation lies at the heart of many clients' problems. Self-indulgence and its sibling self-absorption (McKenzie and Hoyle) can be damaging, but self-control can be learned.

Ego depletion and the muscle analogy. Baumeister and colleagues found that efforts at self-control are psychologically costly ('ego depletion'), but regular self-regulation exercises improve self-regulation, like strengthening a muscle.

Self-control as a subset. VanDellen, Hoyle and Miller distinguish self-control from broader self-regulation: self-control is self-regulation that is both effortful and conscious. A self-regulatory task depleted resources only when it required sustained effort. They also hold that self-control can be learned.

Contagion. VanDellen and Hoyle found self-control can be 'contagious': watching someone exercise self-control makes it easier later, and even thinking of a friend with good self-control helps people stay in control.

Implications. Helping clients find ways to stay in control is more useful than just getting them to recognise and challenge self-indulgent habits. Many clients will struggle with self-regulation, and if they are to take responsibility and stay in the driver's seat they may need help with self-control.
sections.simple: Self-control is central to taking responsibility for yourself, and lack of it often lies behind clients' problems. Research shows self-control uses up energy (ego depletion) but gets stronger with practice like a muscle, and can even be 'caught' from others. Helpers should help clients find ways to stay in control.
