sections.heading: A Bias for Action as an Outcome-Focused Value; The Need for Behavioral Activation
sections.detailed:
If life-enhancing outcomes are central to helping, so is the behaviour that produces them. Clients must ultimately engage, directly or indirectly, in internal (thinking) and external (action) behaviour that creates outcomes.

Behavioral activation (BA). Sometimes called activity scheduling, BA is a treatment for depression built on this principle. Devised years ago (Jacobson), it has had a renaissance of sorts (Coffman and colleagues, Cuijpers and colleagues, Hopko and colleagues, and others). BA targets inertia and avoidance. Hopko and colleagues state its premise: increased activity and the resulting contact with positive consequences are enough to reduce depressive symptoms and increase positive thoughts and feelings.

BA involves helping clients monitor mood and daily activities, identify rewarding activities, schedule pleasant activities and increase their number, increase positive interactions with the environment, move from easier to harder tasks, reward progress, and review and maintain gains; in short, moving clients into action beyond inertia and avoidance. Cuijpers, van Straten and Warmerdam's meta-analysis found activity scheduling effective, and noted it is attractive because it is uncomplicated, time-efficient and does not require complex skills from patient or therapist.

Why only a renaissance 'of sorts'? A real renaissance would stress clients acting on their own behalf in all problem situations. BA is not limited to depression; an action component is needed in all problem management.

Agency. The overall goal from Chapter 1 is helping clients become more effective agents in helping and in daily life: doers rather than reactors, preventers rather than fixers, initiators rather than followers. Egan's example is Lawrence, valued by superiors because he was competent and did whatever they wanted, being moved from job to job without complaint. As he matured he took to heart the adage that if you are not in charge of your career, no one is. After career counselling he presented his desired career path, showing how it served both the company and himself; his superiors, taken aback, agreed, and when they later sidetracked him he stood up for his rights. Assertiveness was his bias for action.

The doer is more likely to pursue 'stretch' rather than merely adaptive goals and to move beyond problem management to opportunity development. Bandura, focusing on human agency, argues the helping professions under-emphasise personal agency. Angus and Kagan link empathy and action: when helpers respond empathically to clients describing what they have done to bring about change, they encourage the client's sense of agency, which they call 'empathic validation'.
sections.simple: Outcomes come from action, so helpers should have a bias for action. Behavioral activation, a treatment for depression, gets clients doing rewarding activities to beat inertia and avoidance, and it works. Egan wants this action focus in all helping, so clients become doers and initiators rather than passive reactors.

sections.heading: Action and Discretionary Change
sections.detailed:
To become more effective agents, clients need to understand the difference between discretionary and nondiscretionary change. Nondiscretionary change is mandated: if a court tells a divorced man negotiating visiting rights that he cannot see his children unless he stops drinking, there will be no visits without change. Discretionary change is not forced: a couple with marital difficulties is not under the gun to change; the message is 'IF you want a better relationship, THEN you must change in these ways'.

Egan says the fact of discretionary change is central to mediocrity. If we do not have to change, we often do not, as the track record of New Year's resolutions shows. Clients often see change as discretionary; they may talk as though it is required, but underneath runs the feeling 'I don't really have to change; others and the world should change'. Egan stresses this is not cynicism but realism, meant to make helpers realistic about the challenges they and their clients face.

A pragmatic bias toward client action, rather than mere talk about action, is a cardinal value. Effective helpers are active, see no value in mere listening and nodding, and engage clients in dialogue, constantly asking what they can do to raise the probability that the client will act intelligently and prudently on his or her own behalf. Egan's cautionary example: a man went 'into therapy' partly for indecisiveness and, over years, got engaged several times and broke each engagement off; so much for decisiveness.
sections.simple: Nondiscretionary change is forced (e.g. by a court); discretionary change is optional, and people often avoid it, like broken New Year's resolutions. Clients often feel they do not really have to change, so helpers must actively push toward action rather than just listen and nod.

sections.heading: Real-Life Focus
sections.detailed:
For clients to make progress they must do better in their day-to-day lives. The focus of helping is therefore not narrowly on sessions and client-helper interactions but on clients managing everyday life more effectively.

Egan tells of a friend who, early in his career, was delighted with the solid relationship he was building with a client until, in the third interview, she told him he was full of himself and that they were not getting anywhere. He had become so absorbed in relationship building that he forgot her pressing everyday concerns.

Hanna, working with difficult clients, developed a model of change that emphasises clients as active agents. He argues the behaviourist view of human beings overemphasises mechanistic and deterministic factors and so shortchanges clients. Bohart and Tallman say clients, to varying degrees, can solve their own problems, generate ideas and actively contribute to therapy. Egan goes further: clients not only can, they must.
sections.simple: Helping is about clients doing better in real life, not just about good sessions. A helper who focuses only on the relationship can forget the client's actual problems. Clients are active agents who can and must contribute to their own change.
keyPoints: Progress means doing better in day-to-day life, not just in sessions.
Cautionary tale: a helper lost in relationship building.

Egan: clients not only can but must.

sections.heading: Shadow-Side Realities in the Helping Relationship; Helpers' and Clients' Flaws
sections.detailed:
Like any relationship, the helper-client relationship can go wrong in many ways. Egan samples these shadow-side realities.

Helpers' flaws. Helping relationships often fall short of the chapter's ideals, and helpers' motives are not always pure. Helpers find clients attractive or unattractive, which is not wrong in itself, but they must manage closeness in a way that furthers helping (R. S. Schwartz) and handle both positive and negative feelings, lest they do silly things. They may need to resist being less challenging with attractive clients or listening less carefully to unattractive ones. Some helpers lack commitment in a profession that demands it. And helpers, like others, get into trouble but often fail to use their own tools to get out of it: 'Don't do as I do; do as I say.'

Clients' flaws. Some clients have unrealistic expectations of counselling (Tinsley, Bowman and Barich); others are tripped up by distorted views of their helpers, so helpers must manage expectations and the relationship. Clients play games with themselves, their helpers and the process. Helpers sometimes seduce clients and clients seduce helpers, not necessarily sexually. Both may pursue hidden agendas. The relationship can even become a conspiracy to do nothing.

Being neither naive nor cynical. Neither helpers nor clients are usually heroes; they have all-too-human tendencies. We now talk openly about human defects without descending into cynicism. Needleman asks why people repeatedly violate their deepest values; Hollis asks why good people do bad things and explores humanity's darker side; Ford asks the same and suggests how to stop being our own worst enemies; Martinez-Lewi discusses freeing ourselves from narcissism. The dark side is often as close as the end of one's nose. The trick is to be neither naive nor cynical about yourself or your clients.
sections.simple: Real helping relationships have flaws. Helpers may be swayed by attraction, lack commitment or not practise what they preach. Clients may have unrealistic expectations, play games or have hidden agendas, and the pair may even 'conspire' to do nothing. The answer is to be neither naive nor cynical.
keyPoints: Helpers' motives are not always pure; manage attraction and closeness (R. S. Schwartz).
Some helpers lack commitment or don't use their own tools ('Don't do as I do').

The relationship can become a 'conspiracy to do nothing'.
Be neither naive nor cynical (Needleman, Hollis, Ford, Martinez-Lewi).

sections.heading: Incompetent Helpers
sections.detailed:
Some helpers are competent and others are not, yet incompetent helpers pass themselves off as professionals, just as there are good and bad teachers, social workers, managers, police officers and ministers. Helpers who underestimate the severity of problems, have interpersonal difficulties with clients, use poor techniques, overuse a technique or disagree with clients about methods can make things worse. Clients, aided by helpers, work on the wrong issues; helpers fail to keep up with the profession and use methods unlikely to help; helping continues though it is going nowhere. So there is evidence that therapy sometimes makes things worse: some helping leads to negative outcomes.

Even competent, committed helpers have lapses. Luborsky and associates found that:
- therapists differ considerably in their average success rates;
- outcomes vary considerably within an individual therapist's caseload;
- variations in success usually have more to do with the therapist than with the type of treatment.

Helping usually works, but ineffective helping abounds. Helping is powerful and easy to mismanage, and some clients get worse because of inept helpers. Helping is not neutral; it is for better or for worse.

Albert Ellis claimed inept helpers are either ineffective or inefficient. The inefficient may eventually help, but with inept methods that produce weak, short-lived results and waste enormous time and money. Because efficacy studies rarely separate high-level from low-level helpers, and deterioration research suggests many low-level helpers exist, the negative results in many studies are predictable. Finally, little has been written about how helpers deal with failure in therapy (Stewart and Chambless).

Egan closes by noting that Part II (communication and relationship-building skills) and Part III (the problem-management and opportunity-development framework) follow, and the spirit of Chapters 1 and 2 runs through both.
sections.simple: Not all helpers are competent, and bad helping can make clients worse. Luborsky found success depends more on the therapist than on the type of therapy. Ellis said inept helpers are either ineffective or inefficient, and little is written about how helpers handle failure.

practice.answer: The working alliance is the collaborative partnership between client and helper. Norcross describes it as the quality and strength of their collaboration, and Bordin defines it as collaboration based on agreement on the goals and tasks of counselling. Egan uses it to combine the value of the relationship in itself with its use as a means to outcomes.

Drawing on Argyris, espoused values are the ideals a person says they hold, while values-in-use are the behavioural maps they actually use, more or less consistently, to make decisions and guide behaviour. There is often a gap between the two in both clients and helpers, and some values-in-use lead to life-limiting outcomes.

Proposed by Hays, ADDRESSING is an acronym for Age, Developmental and acquired Disabilities, Religion, Ethnicity, Socioeconomic status, Sexual orientation, Indigenous heritage and Gender. It helps therapists recognise, understand and address diversity and multiculturalism in a multidimensional way.

Nondiscretionary change is mandated, for example a court refusing visiting rights unless a man stops drinking. Discretionary change is optional: 'if you want a better relationship, then you must change'. Egan notes that discretionary change is often avoided, which makes it central to mediocrity.

Behavioral activation, or activity scheduling, is a treatment for depression devised by Jacobson. It targets inertia and avoidance by helping clients monitor mood and activity, schedule rewarding activities and move from easier to harder tasks. Its premise is that more activity and contact with positive consequences reduce depression.

practice.q: Explain the three types of client collaboration identified by Bachelor and colleagues and the guiding principles for alliance behaviour.
practice.answer:
Egan sees helping as a two-person team effort in which both helper and client share responsibility for outcomes. Bachelor, Laverdiere, Gamache and Bordeleau examined what collaboration means to clients and found three types. Active clients see themselves as playing a significant role in whether therapy moves forward. Mutual clients acknowledge their own role but expect the therapist to play an equally active role. Therapist-dependent clients see collaboration as the therapist's beneficial interventions; about a third of clients were of this type, and Egan suggests this is really cooperation rather than collaboration.

Because the alliance is an abstraction, it becomes real through behaviour. Egan's guiding principles are: alliances emerge from collaborative work rather than being built directly; helpers should track clients' evolving needs and preferences and adjust (Laura does not push Karl to accept surveys); focus on clients' resources and strengths from the start; expect helper and client to view the relationship differently, especially early; accept ups and downs as normal, since Horvath and colleagues link resolved fluctuations with good outcomes; and expect and handle client negativity without taking it personally, as when Karl tells Laura she knows nothing about war. Together these principles turn the idea of collaboration into everyday practice.

practice.q: Discuss the behaviours that show respect and disrespect towards clients.
practice.answer:
Egan calls respect the foundation value of helping. Its Latin root refers to seeing, and it is a way of viewing others that must show in behaviour; Rogers called it positive regard with nonpossessive warmth.

Disrespect: first, doing harm. 'Do no harm' is the first rule of helpers, yet unprincipled or incompetent helpers harm clients, since helping is for better or for worse; a non-manipulative, non-exploitative stance is essential. Second, rushing to judgement. Helpers should help clients explore the consequences of their values rather than condemn them; in Egan's example, the respectful counsellor reflects an arrogant client's priority on frankness without judging or condoning.

Respect: become competent and committed, since there is no place for the caring incompetent; be genuine, as in Gelso's real relationship, avoiding phoniness and hiding behind the professional role; make it clear you are 'for' the client, caring in a tough-minded, non-sentimental way without simply taking sides; assume the client's goodwill, treating reluctance as something to understand rather than ill will; and keep the client's agenda in focus. Egan's three cautionary cases, a helper absorbed in theories of depression, one who dismissed grief over a pet, and one more interested in politics than the client, show what happens when helpers pursue their own agenda.

practice.q: Explain empathy as a 'two-way street' with reference to Clark's principles.
practice.answer:
Traditional empathy pictures one helper trying to understand one client. Pedersen, Crethar and Carlson argue that empathy at its best is relationship-oriented, and Zaki, Bolger and Ochsner showed that empathic accuracy depends on how both people communicate. Pedersen calls this inclusive cultural empathy.

Janet Clark similarly reconceptualised empathy, defining culture broadly as the traits that make individuals different and using ethnographic ideas to focus on each client's unique frame of reference rather than a group's. Her principles contrast one-way individualistic empathy with two-way relationship empathy: the client's reality is knowable but the helper's understanding is always partial and fallible; helpers must attune to the cultural meaning of words, not just feelings; empathy covers key contexts of the client's life, including social location, their sociopolitical environment and status; regarding cultural uniqueness, the helper is a learner, not an expert; the client's inductive self-understanding matters more than the helper's theory-based deductions; empathy is produced mutually through dialogue; and self-awareness of bias is not enough without ongoing self-reflexivity about fears, mistakes and breakthroughs in sessions. The upshot is that understanding is co-created, not handed over by the helper.

practice.q: Describe the working charter and why helping should not be a 'black box'.
practice.answer:
Many relationships, such as marriage and friendship, are governed by explicit or implicit contracts. If helping is collaborative, both parties must understand their responsibilities. Egan prefers 'working charter' to 'contract' because it avoids legal overtones and suggests a cooperative venture.

The charter should cover eight elements: the nature and goals of helping; an overview of the approach and techniques; the flexibility built into the process; how the process will help clients reach their goals; relevant information about the helper; how the relationship is structured and each party's responsibilities; the values driving helping; and procedural issues such as session place and length and rules about contact between sessions. Manthei and Miller wrote a practical book on charters for clients, and there is some evidence they help even seriously mentally ill clients.

Helping should not be a black box because clients have a right to know what they are getting into. Helpers can explain the process, give a simple pamphlet, or use a short orientation video like that of Reis and Brown. Details can be shared over several sessions so distressed clients are not overwhelmed; clients should be told as much as they can reasonably assimilate. Sharing the process is itself an empowerment norm.

practice.q: Write a note on self-regulation and self-control as part of self-responsibility.
practice.answer:
Egan treats self-regulation, or self-control, as a key part of self-responsibility. Baumeister and colleagues define self-regulation as an adaptive, distinctively human trait that lets people override and change their responses to meet social and other standards. Related is conscientiousness, which Bogg and Roberts define as the tendency to control impulses, be task- and goal-oriented, plan, delay gratification and follow rules; conscientious people live longer and healthier lives.

Lack of self-control often lies at the heart of clients' problems. Druckerman controversially suggests French children behave better because they are indulged less, and Egan notes that self-indulgence and self-absorption (McKenzie and Hoyle) can be damaging. However, self-control can be learned. Baumeister found self-control efforts are costly (ego depletion) but regular practice strengthens self-regulation like a muscle. VanDellen, Hoyle and Miller treat self-control as the effortful, conscious subset of self-regulation, which depletes resources only when sustained effort is needed. VanDellen and Hoyle found self-control is contagious: watching, or even thinking about, someone with good self-control helps.

For helpers, the implication is that helping clients find ways to stay in control is more useful than just pointing out bad habits, so that clients can get into and stay in the driver's seat.

practice.q: Discuss the different views of the helping relationship. How does the working alliance integrate them, and how can the relationship itself be a vehicle for change?
practice.answer:
Introduction
Everyone in counselling agrees the helper-client relationship matters, but Egan shows they differ on how it should be understood and used. Some stress the relationship itself, others the work done through it, and the vocabulary ranges from 'relationship' to 'working alliance'. Egan does not try to settle the debate; he wants helpers to gain a clinical feel for a good relationship, remembering that each helper and client must co-discover the right way for their encounter.

The relationship in itself
Each party brings personality traits and a personal culture that shape how they relate, and Norcross reminds us that the relationship is broader than the alliance. Carl Rogers, representing the humanistic-experiential approach, held that unconditional positive regard, accurate empathy and genuineness, offered by the helper and perceived by the client, are necessary and often sufficient for change. For Rogers the relationship is a facilitative condition. Psychodynamic approaches instead centre on transference and countertransference, unconscious dynamics rooted in the past that must be worked through.

The relationship as a means to an end
Cognitive and behavioural practitioners value the relationship because it enables the work. Tursi and Cochran note that cognitive-behavioural tasks occur within a person-centred relational frame. Overstressing the relationship distracts from the real goal of managing problems and developing opportunities, though a poor relationship will still block success.

The working alliance as integration
Norcross defines the alliance as the quality and strength of collaboration; Bordin as collaboration based on agreement on goals and tasks; Horvath and colleagues as an emergent partnership. It joins the empathic relationship with the outcome focus. Helping becomes a two-person team effort in which helpers do not cure clients and both share responsibility. Bachelor and colleagues found active, mutual and therapist-dependent collaboration. Egan's alliance principles include letting alliances emerge, tracking client needs, focusing on resources, expecting differing views and ups and downs, and handling client negativity. Research by Bedi and by Ackerman and Hilsenroth shows clients value warmth, honesty, validation and even a smiling greeting. Getting off to a good start matters because early change predicts outcome (Miller, Duncan et al.).

The relationship as a vehicle for change
Mallinckrodt describes the relationship as a forum for social-emotional relearning. Helpers model attitudes clients can adopt: a client who feels cared for may learn to care for himself. In the safety of sessions, shy clients speak up and aggressive ones back off, and they transfer this learning to outside relationships. Flexibility is essential: one perfect relationship for all is a myth, and helpers tailor warmth and style (A. A. Lazarus; Mahrer). Duncan, Miller and Sparks go further, arguing clients make therapy work and helpers should follow their lead. Ruptures (Eubanks-Carter, Muran and Safran) can become opportunities for growth.

Conclusion
Egan's position is that the relationship is both valuable in itself and a means to life-enhancing outcomes. The working alliance captures both, and through modelling, safe experimentation and repair of ruptures, the relationship becomes a powerful vehicle for change, provided it stays tailored to each client and focused on real-life results.

practice.q: Explain the five values that drive the helping relationship according to Egan.
practice.answer:
Introduction
Egan argues that the best way to characterise a helping relationship is through the values that drive it; the relationship is the vehicle through which values come alive. Values-in-use are practical tools for decisions, and helpers without explicit values fall back on an implicit default set. Drawing on the tradition of the helping professions, he proposes five values, while urging helpers to debate them and make them their own.

1. Respect: the foundation value
Respect, from a root meaning 'seeing', is a way of viewing clients that must show in behaviour; Rogers called it positive regard. Helpers show disrespect by doing harm or rushing to judgement. They show respect by being competent and committed, genuine rather than phony, clearly 'for' the client in a tough-minded way, assuming the client's goodwill, and keeping the client's agenda in focus.

2. Empathy: the primary orientation value
Empathy is understanding clients from their point of view, in context, and communicating this when helpful. It has been seen as a trait, a state and a staged process (Barrett-Lennard). Kohut, Covey and Goleman describe its importance, and WAVE Trust research found empathy is the greatest inhibitor of violence. Pedersen and Clark present it as a two-way, culturally inclusive process. As a value it is a radical commitment to understand the client's viewpoint, the client's context and the dissonance between viewpoint and reality.

3. Proactive appreciation of diversity
Diversity is part of respect and empathy, and its essence is client factors: 'it's about clients'. Culture is shared beliefs and values producing norms and behaviour patterns; personal culture is 'the way I live my life'. Helpers need diversity competence: understanding diversity (Hays's ADDRESSING), challenging blind spots, tailoring interventions and working with individuals, since differences within groups can exceed those between groups. The Cultural Competence Continuum and Egan's adapted competencies guide practice.

4. Self-responsibility: the empowerment value
Helpers do not empower clients; they help clients find and use their own power. Since helping is a social-influence process (Strong; Corrigan), helpers must influence without taking away responsibility. Norms include believing clients can change, not seeing them as victims or fragile, sharing the process through a working charter, treating sessions as work, acting as a coach, accepting two-way influence and focusing on learning. Conscientiousness and self-regulation, which can be strengthened like a muscle, support self-responsibility.

5. A bias for action: the outcome value
Outcomes require action. Behavioral activation shows the power of moving clients beyond inertia and avoidance, and Egan wants this in all problem management. Clients often treat change as discretionary, so helpers must actively raise the probability that clients will act, and keep the focus on real life rather than the sessions alone.

Conclusion
Together these values form a coherent package: respect as foundation, empathy as orientation, diversity as openness to the world as it is, self-responsibility as empowerment and action as the route to outcomes. Egan treats them as a starting point that helpers must examine and make their own.

practice.q: Critically discuss Egan's view of diversity and multicultural competence in counselling.
practice.answer:
Introduction
Egan treats proactive appreciation of diversity as a core helping value, part of respect and empathy and linked to empowerment. His central message is that the diversity focus highlights client factors as the key to successful therapy: it is not about culture as such, but about clients.

Upsides and downsides
The literature has exploded. Its benefits are that it forces helpers to confront blind spots and that exposure to many cultures may enhance creativity (Leung and colleagues). Its risks are that multiculturalism can become a fad and an industry that diverts attention from individual clients, and Putnam found diverse communities trust less in the short term; mere contact is not enough.

Culture and personal culture
Bronfenbrenner called culture the most controlling system. Egan defines it as shared beliefs and values producing shared norms and behaviour patterns, and applies it to individuals as personal culture. Isaiah's beliefs (the world is heartless), values (security), norms (do not trust) and behaviour (staying a loner) illustrate this. People personalise group culture (Massimini and Delle Fave), so they are never carbon copies. The case of Sue, Patrick and their counsellor Antonio, together with Guisinger and Blatt's contrast between self-development and relatedness, shows how cultural values can clash in counselling.

Helper competencies
Diversity competence is the knowledge and skill to work with anyone significantly different. Day lists awareness, knowledge and skills, though no package is universally agreed. Egan's guidelines are: understand diversity contextually (Hays's ADDRESSING); challenge blind spots; tailor interventions, for example around self-disclosure; and work with individuals. Satel says therapy is about individuals, not groups, and there are as many differences within groups as between them. The Cultural Competence Continuum runs from destructiveness to proficiency, and Egan's adapted list covers self-awareness, sociopolitical influences, limits of Western methods, culture-specific versus universal issues and non-biased treatment planning.

Critical evaluation
The strength of Egan's view is its balance. He accepts the importance of culture but warns that category traits can destroy understanding as well as aid it and that, pushed too far, diversity principles would make helping anyone impossible. He openly states his bias toward personal culture and rejects over-complex tools such as the 60-question cultural audit, siding with Stuart that no one has a pure culture and it is never safe to infer orientation from group membership. Critics might say this emphasis on the individual could underplay structural factors, though Egan does list sociopolitical influences such as oppression and marginalisation among the competencies. His admission that multiculturalism solves some problems and raises others is honest rather than dismissive.

Conclusion
For Egan, diversity competence means understanding groups well enough to adapt to the individual, being aware of one's own biases, and engaging each client's personal culture. In his words, understand the client in any way you can, but work with the individual.

practice.q: Discuss helping as a social-influence process and the norms that support client empowerment.
practice.answer:
Introduction
Egan frames self-responsibility as an empowerment-focused value. Client responsibility assumes clients have the power to do what is right for themselves and others. Helpers do not hand out power; they help clients discover and use their own. Because clients experience helpers as powerful and all helpers influence clients, the issue of social influence must be faced.

Helping as social influence
Influence is everywhere; Smith and Mackie count it among basic principles of behaviour, and Crano calls it the hallmark of social psychology. Rashotte separates social influence, real change through interaction with people seen as similar, desirable or expert, from conformity, power and authority. Clients dislike influence experienced as power because it can become manipulation (McCarthy and Frieze). Strong's article on counselling as interpersonal influence sparked research, and Corrigan's review concluded simply that counsellors are influential. Perrin and colleagues note that the diversity movement has shifted influence toward reciprocal, collegial forms. Egan's point is that helpers can influence without robbing clients of responsibility.

The influence continuum
Influence ranges from directing clients' lives to leaving them entirely alone. Thaler and Sunstein argue the latter is impossible because nudging is unavoidable. Most helping lies between, at 'helping clients make and act on their own decisions'. Preventing suicide sits near the controlling end; passively accepting avoidance near the other. Hare-Mustin and Marecek describe the tension between self-determination and the helper's duty to help.

Norms for empowerment
Freire warned that helping must not become another form of oppression. Egan's norms, partly from Farrelly and Brandsma, are:
- Start from the premise that clients can change if they choose, helping them free and realistically assess their resources.
- Do not see clients as victims; work with whatever freedom remains.
- Do not be fooled by appearances, as the dismissed trainee who became a star shows.
- Share the helping process through a working charter covering goals, approach, roles, values and procedures, so helping is not a black box.
- Help clients see sessions as work sessions.
- Act as a coach or consultant (Mee-Lee and colleagues) who influences while leaving decisions with the client.
- Accept helping as two-way influence, as in Tyler, Pargament and Gatz's resource collaborator role and Timothy learning from Wei-Lian.
- Focus on learning: Howell links learning to increasing viable options.
- Do not see clients as overly fragile; client deference (Rennie) is not fragility, and Driscoll urges earlier challenge.
Cultural differences matter, as Lin's study of Taiwanese students' self-reliance shows, but ultimately it is this client's approach that counts.

Conclusion
Influence in helping is inevitable; the question is its direction and purpose. Egan's norms ensure influence is collaborative and empowering, so clients leave with more resources and responsibility rather than more dependency.

practice.q: What are the shadow-side realities of the helping relationship? Discuss with reference to incompetent helpers.
practice.answer:
Introduction
After describing an ideal relationship driven by respect, empathy, diversity, empowerment and action, Egan honestly admits that, like any relationship, helping can go wrong. He calls these the shadow-side realities and samples them under two headings: the flaws of helpers and clients, and incompetent helpers.

Helpers' flaws
Helpers' motives are not always pure. They find some clients attractive and others not; this is normal, but they must manage closeness so that it serves helping (R. S. Schwartz) and handle both positive and negative feelings. They may challenge attractive clients less or listen less carefully to unattractive ones. Some lack commitment in a profession that demands it, and many fail to apply their own tools to their own troubles, a 'don't do as I do, do as I say' attitude.

Clients' flaws
Some clients have unrealistic expectations of counselling (Tinsley, Bowman and Barich), and others hold distorted views of their helpers, so helpers must manage expectations and the relationship. Clients play games with themselves, their helpers and the process. Helpers and clients may seduce each other, not necessarily sexually, and both may pursue hidden agendas. At worst the relationship becomes a conspiracy to do nothing.

A realistic stance
Neither party is heroic; both are all too human. Egan cites writers who explore human failings: Needleman on violating one's values, Hollis and Ford on why good people do bad things, Martinez-Lewi on narcissism. The dark side may be as close as the end of one's nose. The key is to be neither naive nor cynical about oneself or clients.

Incompetent helpers
Some helpers are incompetent yet pass as professionals. They underestimate problem severity, struggle interpersonally, use poor or overused techniques, argue with clients about methods, work on the wrong issues, fail to keep up with the field and continue helping that is going nowhere. As a result some helping produces negative outcomes. Even competent helpers lapse: Luborsky and associates found that therapists differ considerably in average success, outcomes vary within each therapist's caseload, and success depends more on the therapist than on the type of treatment. Albert Ellis said inept helpers are either ineffective or inefficient, the latter producing weak, short-lived results at great cost of time and money. Because efficacy studies seldom separate high- and low-level helpers, negative findings are predictable, and little has been written on how helpers handle failure (Stewart and Chambless).

Conclusion
The shadow side reminds helpers that helping is not neutral but 'for better or for worse'. Recognising flaws in oneself and clients, and committing to competence, is itself an expression of the respect that Egan places at the foundation of helping.

summary: Everyone agrees the relationship matters, but views differ on whether it is valuable in itself or a means to an end.
Rogers held that positive regard, accurate empathy and genuineness are necessary and often sufficient; psychodynamic approaches focus on transference and countertransference.
The working alliance (Bordin: agreement on goals and tasks) integrates both views; helping is a two-person team effort.
Alliances emerge from collaborative work; early change matters, so a good start (positive expectancies, active client role, collaborative goals) is important.
Clients value warmth, honesty, validation and small strengths-fostering behaviours; client views deserve more attention (Bedi).
The relationship is a forum for relearning, and no single relationship style fits all clients; ruptures can become opportunities.
Values-in-use are tools of the trade; helpers must examine and own their values.
Respect is the foundation value: do no harm, don't rush to judgement; be competent, genuine, 'for' the client, assume goodwill, follow the client's agenda.
Empathy is the primary orientation value: a radical commitment to understand the client's viewpoint, context and the gap between view and reality; at its best it is two-way.
Diversity is about clients: understand personal culture, challenge blind spots, tailor interventions and work with individuals.
Helpers do not empower clients but help them use their own power; influence is inevitable and should be collaborative.
Empowerment norms include working charters, sessions as work, coaching, two-way influence and not treating clients as victims or fragile.
Conscientiousness and self-control support self-responsibility; self-control can be learned and is even contagious.
A bias for action is the outcome value; behavioral activation shows the power of action, and discretionary change is easily avoided.
The shadow side includes flawed motives, games, hidden agendas and incompetent helpers; helping is 'for better or for worse'.
